removed.title: Ramnagar Decision Cards
removed.text:
Card 1: Install rooftop solar panels on the school.
Card 2: Plant a community forest on the deforested hillside.
Card 3: Build a small stepwell to harvest monsoon rain.
Card 4: Switch the brick kilns from coal to natural gas.
Card 5: Introduce CNG three-wheelers for transport.
Card 6: Create a village compost pit using fallen leaves.
Card 7: Use wind energy to pump water from the existing well.
Card 8: Quarry the local granite ridge for new construction material.
Card 9: Ask residents to fix all household tap leaks.
Card 10: Organise a Van Mahotsav tree-planting drive.
Card 11: Install a solar water heater at the community centre.
Card 12: Restrict the number of trees felled each year.

Groups must choose at least seven cards and may choose all twelve. Every chosen card requires a written justification. Each of Ramnagar's six problems must be matched to at least one chosen card — this prevents groups from avoiding uncomfortable options.

periods.activity_title: Breath, Wind, and Water — First Encounters
periods.activity_description: Students perform the breath-holding exercise from Activity 11.1, recording bodily responses, then construct a firki pinwheel (Activity 11.2) and observe how moving air causes rotation. They close by examining a cup of water and listing every property they can detect with their senses.

roles.role_description: Guides the breath-holding and firki construction, prompting students to record observations rather than jump to explanations.
Performs the breath-holding exercise and records bodily discomfort, then constructs the firki and records the rotation observation.
Shares firki observations with a partner and jointly lists properties of water they can detect by sight, touch, and smell.

time_bands.activity: Each student holds their breath and notes when discomfort begins, recording the experience in a two-column table: 'What I did' and 'What I felt'.
Students fold paper pinwheels following the firki instructions and hold them in moving air, recording in a sentence what the rotation shows about moving air.
Students examine a small cup of water and list every observable property — colour, feel, smell, whether it takes the shape of the container — in their notebooks.
Pairs share their water-property lists aloud; the teacher captures a class list on the board for reference in the next unit.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit opens the chapter by letting students meet three resources — air, wind, and water — through direct sensory experience before any vocabulary is introduced. Watch for students who say they 'don't feel anything' during the breath exercise; gently ask whether they could hold it longer and why not, drawing out that the body signals its need for oxygen. The class list of water properties built at the close gives a shared reference that every subsequent unit can point back to.
materials: Plain A4 paper for firki construction
Scissors
Pins or pencil tips for pinwheel pivot
Small cups of water (one per pair)

periods.activity_title: Soil Colours and Textures — A Close Look
periods.activity_description: Students carry out Activity 11.4, examining soil samples collected from two or three different locations around the school. Using the naked eye and a magnifying lens they record colour, texture, and any visible particles in an observation table, noting that soils from different places look and feel different.

roles.role_description: Distributes pre-collected soil samples in labelled cups and models how to use a magnifying lens safely and systematically.
Examines each labelled soil sample in turn, completing an observation table with colour and texture entries for every sample.

time_bands.activity: The teacher briefly recaps the previous unit's class water-property list, then introduces soil as a third resource students will observe today, distributing labelled cups of soil samples.

Groups examine each sample — first with the naked eye, then under the magnifying lens — and fill in the observation table: Sample label | Colour | Texture (rough/smooth/gritty) | Anything else noticed.
Each group chooses its most surprising difference between two samples and prepares a single sentence to share with the class.
Groups share their sentences; the teacher notes recurring observations on the board and asks: 'What might cause soils from different places to look different?' — holding answers for the next unit.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit builds directly on the sensory-observation practice from the previous unit, now applying it to soil. A common slip is students labelling soil as simply 'dirty brown' for every sample; prompt them with 'Is this brown the same shade as that one?' and 'Does this one feel different between your fingers?' to sharpen their descriptive precision. Ending with an open question about what causes the differences primes curiosity for the rock-and-mineral content that comes in later units.
materials: Labelled cups of soil samples from 2–3 school locations (collected by teacher beforehand)
Magnifying lenses (one per group)
Observation table printed or drawn in notebooks

periods.activity_title: Fuels Around Us — A Neighbourhood Survey
periods.activity_description: Students carry out Activity 11.5 by recalling and listing the types of vehicles and cooking appliances familiar to them, then recording which fuel each uses in a survey table. They also observe what happens visually when a vehicle exhaust or a burning candle releases smoke.

roles.role_description: Introduces the survey table structure and prompts students to recall vehicles and cooking devices from daily life rather than inventing new ones.
Completes the survey table independently, listing at least five vehicles or appliances and the fuel each uses, then sketches or describes the visible sign of burning.
Compares tables with neighbours to check for items missed and adds any new entries before whole-class sharing.

time_bands.activity: The teacher connects to the previous two units: 'We observed air and soil as resources — today we look at a resource that powers things around us.' Students brainstorm fuels they have seen or heard of at home.
Students independently complete the survey table: Vehicle or appliance | Fuel used | How they know (seen, heard, smelled).
Pairs compare tables and add any missing entries; they circle fuels that appear in more than three rows, noting which are most common.
Whole-class share: teacher lists the circled fuels on the board — petrol, diesel, CNG, LPG — and students note any fuels they did not include, setting up the next unit's classification work.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit completes the observation stage by turning students' everyday environment into data. Watch for students who list 'gas' as a fuel without distinguishing LPG from CNG; note the difference briefly but defer explanation to the next unit so observation stays the focus here. The board list of common fuels at the close gives a concrete data set the class will use in Stage 2 when classifying resources.
materials: Survey table template (drawn in notebook or on a printed sheet)
Board or chart paper for class fuel list

periods.stage_label: Classify resources by origin and replenishment
periods.activity_title: Where Does Each Resource Come From?
periods.activity_description: Students receive a set of resource cards — air, water, sunlight, forest, soil, coal, petroleum, and minerals — and sort them by asking two guided questions: 'Does nature provide this directly?' and 'How long does it take nature to make more of it?' They record their preliminary groupings and justify each placement in writing.

roles.role_description: Poses the two sorting questions, circulates to push groups whose justifications are vague, and refrains from correcting groupings until after sharing.
Sorts resource cards into provisional groups using the two guiding questions and writes a one-sentence justification for each card's placement.

time_bands.activity: The teacher recalls the board list of fuels and the soil observation table from previous units and introduces the two sorting questions, distributing resource cards to groups.
Groups sort cards and write justifications; the teacher circulates, asking 'How long do you think it takes for coal to form?' and 'Can the wind be used up?' to deepen reasoning.
Each group shares one placement they found difficult to decide; the teacher records contested cards on the board without resolving them.
The teacher introduces the terms 'renewable' and 'non-renewable' from Section 11.7 and asks students to revise their groupings accordingly, flagging any card they are still unsure about.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit begins Stage 2, shifting from observation to classification; build on the resource list and fuel survey from the previous three units by naming them explicitly as the data set being sorted. Students frequently misplace forests as non-renewable because 'trees get cut'; probe with 'Can a new forest grow? How long does that take compared to how long coal takes?' to surface the replenishment-rate criterion. Ending with contested cards on the board maintains productive uncertainty and motivates the next unit's deeper investigation.
materials: Resource cards (one set per group — words written on paper strips: Air, Water, Sunlight, Forest, Soil, Coal, Petroleum, Natural Gas, Minerals)
Notebook for justifications

periods.stage_label: Classify resources by origin and replenishment
periods.activity_title: Mapping the Chapter's Resources — A Structured Overview
periods.activity_description: The teacher systematically introduces each resource from Sections 11.1 through 11.7, connecting the chapter's content to the renewable or non-renewable classification students began in the previous unit. Students build a structured two-column reference table in their notebooks, recording for each resource: name, source, replenishment time, and renewable or non-renewable label.

roles.role_description: Presents each resource in sequence, links it to students' prior sorting work, and pauses after each resource for students to complete their table row.
Listens, asks clarifying questions, and completes the reference table row by row, including the renewable or non-renewable label with a brief reason.

time_bands.activity: The teacher returns to the contested cards from the previous unit and resolves them by briefly explaining the renewable or non-renewable criterion before beginning the structured overview.

Section by section — air and wind, water, solar energy, forests, soil and rocks, minerals, fossil fuels — the teacher presents the resource, its source, and its replenishment time; students complete their table after each.
Students use their completed table to check whether their original resource card groupings from the previous unit were correct, marking any they need to revise.
Quick oral check: the teacher names a resource at random and students respond with renewable or non-renewable and one reason, giving the teacher a pulse on readiness for the next unit.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit uses a didactic approach to consolidate the classification framework after the inquiry sorting of the previous unit — the structure is deliberate: inquiry first, then direct instruction to resolve and firm up understanding. Watch for students who write 'soil is renewable because it is natural'; the chapter is explicit that soil takes thousands of years to form and is classified as non-renewable, so address this precisely. The completed reference table becomes a tool students will draw on in every subsequent unit, so insist on completeness before moving on.
materials: Board or chart for teacher's structured presentation
Notebooks for student reference table

periods.stage_label: Classify resources by origin and replenishment
periods.activity_title: Resource Audit of a Morning Routine
periods.activity_description: Students carry out Activity 11.6 by mapping a detailed morning routine — waking up, washing, cooking breakfast, travelling to school — and identifying every natural resource directly or indirectly used at each step. They then label each resource on their reference table as renewable or non-renewable.

roles.role_description: Writes out their own morning routine step by step and annotates each step with the natural resource it uses, then labels it from the reference table.
Compares morning-routine maps with two peers, adds resources they missed, and identifies which step in the routine uses the greatest number of non-renewable resources.

time_bands.activity: Students write out their morning routine in six to eight steps, as specifically as possible — not 'breakfast' but 'cooking rice on a gas stove'.
Students annotate each step with the natural resource(s) it uses and label each resource renewable or non-renewable using the reference table from the previous unit.
Groups compare maps, add missing resources, and together identify the step with the highest concentration of non-renewable resource use.

Whole-class share: two or three groups read their 'highest non-renewable' step; the teacher records these on the board, noting which resources appear most frequently — setting up the cause-and-effect reasoning of Stage 3.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit applies the classification from the previous two units to students' own lives, cementing the renewable or non-renewable distinction through personal experience. A frequent gap is students identifying only the obvious fuel (LPG for cooking) and missing the water, soil-grown food, and electricity also involved in the same step; prompt with 'What did the food grow in?' and 'Where did the electricity come from?' The board list of high-use non-renewable resources at the close creates a natural bridge into the next stage's discussion of what happens when those resources are overused.
materials: Reference table from previous unit (in notebooks)
Board for class compilation

periods.stage_label: Explain causes and consequences of resource depletion and pollution
periods.activity_title: What Happens When a Resource Runs Low?
periods.activity_description: Students examine the consequences of overuse for three resources from the chapter — freshwater, fossil fuels, and forests — by reading the relevant sections and answering a cause-and-effect chain prompt: what human action → what resource change → what consequence for people or environment.

roles.role_description: Models the cause-and-effect chain format using the board list of high-use non-renewable resources from the previous unit, then releases students to complete chains for their assigned resource.
Each group is assigned one resource (freshwater, fossil fuels, or forests) and completes three cause-and-effect chains, drawing only on chapter content.

time_bands.activity: The teacher models one complete chain on the board using the fossil fuel example from Section 11.6: 'Burning fossil fuels → releases smoke and carbon dioxide → large-scale air pollution.'
Groups complete three cause-and-effect chains for their assigned resource using chapter sections; they may also use the reference table from the previous unit to check classifications.
Each group reads one chain aloud; the class listens and adds any missing consequence the chapter mentions that the presenting group did not include.
The teacher asks: 'Which resource consequence do you think affects the most people, and why?' — students give a quick verbal response, setting up the next unit's focus on societal dependencies.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit opens Stage 3, moving from classification to causal reasoning. Build explicitly on the board list of high-use non-renewable resources from the previous unit so students see the progression. Students sometimes confuse correlation with causation — 'forests disappear because animals leave' rather than 'trees are cut, so animals lose habitat'; redirect by asking 'What happens first?' The closing question about which consequence affects the most people primes Stage 3's next unit on societal and environmental dependencies.
materials: Chapter sections 11.2, 11.4, and 11.6 (textbook or printed excerpts)
Cause-and-effect chain template in notebooks
Reference table from previous units

periods.stage_label: Explain causes and consequences of resource depletion and pollution
periods.activity_title: Societal Dependencies — Who Needs Which Resource, and Why?
periods.activity_description: The teacher leads a structured discussion tracing societal and environmental dependencies: unequal freshwater access across India, the role of forests in providing food and shelter for wildlife, and the dependence of electricity generation on coal and fossil fuels. Students annotate their reference table with a 'depends on' column.

roles.role_description: Presents each dependency using chapter content — stepwells, Chipko movement, Van Mahotsav, fossil fuel electricity — and pauses for students to annotate.
Adds a 'who or what depends on this resource' annotation to the reference table row for water, forests, and fossil fuels.

time_bands.activity: The teacher recalls the cause-and-effect chains from the previous unit and frames today's focus: not just what changes, but who is affected and how deeply.

Structured presentation: freshwater inequality across India (unequal access, stepwells as community solutions), forests as habitat and food web foundation, fossil fuels as the backbone of electricity and transport — students annotate after each.
Students add a 'depends on' column entry for at least three resources in their reference table, writing one sentence per resource naming the dependent community or ecosystem.
Students share one 'depends on' sentence with a partner and revise if their partner identifies a dependency they missed from the chapter.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit deepens causal reasoning by adding the dimension of societal dependency; connect it explicitly to the cause-and-effect chains from the previous unit so students see dependency as the human face of depletion. A common gap is students naming only human communities as dependents — prompt them with 'Who else lives in a forest?' to include wildlife and insects as named in Section 11.4. The annotated reference table is now a multi-layered tool that will serve students in the evaluation units ahead.
materials: Reference table in notebooks
Board for teacher's structured presentation

periods.stage_label: Explain causes and consequences of resource depletion and pollution
periods.activity_title: Tracing Pollution — From Source to Consequence
periods.activity_description: Students investigate the pollution consequences associated with fossil fuel use (air pollution from burning) and freshwater wastage (shortage and unequal access) by constructing a two-pathway diagram that shows source → release → environmental or social consequence, drawing exclusively on chapter content.

roles.role_description: Constructs a two-pathway diagram in their notebook — one pathway for fossil fuels, one for freshwater — connecting source, human action, release or loss, and consequence.
Circulates and challenges vague consequence labels by asking 'What exactly does the chapter say happens?' and 'Who experiences this consequence?'

time_bands.activity: The teacher recalls the societal dependencies from the previous unit and introduces the diagram format on the board using a blank template: Source → Human Action → Release/Loss → Consequence.

Students construct both pathways independently; they must cite a specific chapter detail for each arrow in the chain — e.g., 'burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide' or 'unequal freshwater access leaves some regions short'.
Students compare their two diagrams with a neighbour and check whether each arrow is supported by a chapter detail; they add or correct any missing links.
The teacher selects two or three diagrams to project or read aloud, highlighting strong specific links and asking the class to suggest improvements for any vague arrows.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit asks students to synthesise causal reasoning across two resource types simultaneously, a step up in cognitive demand from the previous unit's single-resource focus. Watch for students who write 'pollution is bad' as the final consequence node — prompt them to use the chapter's specific language: 'large-scale air pollution' or 'not fit for drinking, agriculture, or industrial use.' Reviewing two or three diagrams aloud at the close gives the class a collective quality standard before they move into evaluation in Stage 4.
materials: Notebooks for diagrams
Board for blank diagram template

periods.stage_label: Evaluate conservation choices and develop informed judgements about responsible consumption
periods.activity_title: Conservation in Practice — What Works and Why?
periods.activity_description: Students examine specific conservation practices described in the chapter — rainwater harvesting, the Chipko movement, Van Mahotsav, using solar energy, walking or cycling instead of driving — and evaluate each by applying two criteria: which resource it conserves, and whether it addresses the cause or only the consequence of depletion.

roles.role_description: Evaluates three assigned conservation practices using the two criteria, completing an evaluation grid and writing a one-sentence verdict on each practice's effectiveness.
Introduces the two evaluation criteria, models the evaluation of one practice (rainwater harvesting) on the board, then steps back as groups work.

time_bands.activity: The teacher introduces the two evaluation criteria and models an evaluation of rainwater harvesting: resource conserved = freshwater; addresses cause or consequence = cause (captures rain before it is lost), drawing on Section 11.2.

Groups evaluate three practices — each group receives a different trio from the chapter's full list — completing the evaluation grid with resource conserved, cause or consequence addressed, and a one-sentence verdict.
Groups share their verdicts; the class discusses whether any practice only treats the symptom and what a more root-cause approach would look like.
The teacher posts a class evaluation grid on the board summarising all practices and their verdicts, which students copy as a reference for the next unit.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit opens Stage 4, the evaluation stage — build on the causal chain reasoning from Stage 3 by framing evaluation as asking 'Does this conservation action reach the cause?' This is a new cognitive move for most students. A common error is rating all conservation actions as equally effective; probe with 'Does planting trees during Van Mahotsav prevent more cutting, or does it repair damage after?' to surface the cause-versus-consequence distinction. The class evaluation grid becomes a shared reference tool for the judgement-writing unit that follows.
materials: Evaluation grid template (drawn in notebooks)
Board for class compilation

periods.stage_label: Evaluate conservation choices and develop informed judgements about responsible consumption
periods.activity_title: Water Wastage Audit — Judging Our Own Use
periods.activity_description: Students revisit Activity 11.3, examining hand washing, cooking, and gardening scenarios to identify specific wastage points. They evaluate current practices against the chapter's conservation strategies — turning off taps, fixing leakages, recycling water, rainwater harvesting — and record a ranked list of changes ordered by impact.

roles.role_description: Identifies three wastage points in the provided scenarios, matches each to a chapter conservation strategy, and ranks the strategies by estimated impact, giving a written justification for the top-ranked choice.
Circulates and presses students to justify their ranking using the chapter's content rather than general intuition — asking 'What does the chapter say about that strategy?'

time_bands.activity: The teacher recalls the class evaluation grid from the previous unit and frames today's activity: 'Let's turn evaluation inward — how well do we use water?'

Students work through Activity 11.3 individually, identifying wastage points in hand-washing, cooking, and gardening scenarios and annotating each with the chapter's recommended conservation strategy.
Students rank the identified strategies from most to least impactful and write a one-paragraph justification for their top-ranked choice, citing chapter content.
Two students share their top-ranked strategy and justification; the class votes on whether the justification is convincing, giving brief verbal reasons for their vote.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit keeps the evaluation lens of Stage 4 but grounds it in students' immediate daily context, making the judgement personal rather than abstract. Students often rank 'fix leakages' first simply because it sounds significant; press for chapter-grounded reasoning by asking 'What evidence from the chapter supports this being the biggest change?' Watch also for students who conflate rainwater harvesting with just 'collecting rain in a bucket' — the chapter describes it as an age-old practice with stepwells and seepage from ponds, so prompt for that fuller picture. The written justification is practice for the extended reasoning expected in Stage 4's final unit.
materials: Textbook Section 11.2 (or printed excerpt)
Class evaluation grid from previous unit

periods.stage_label: Evaluate conservation choices and develop informed judgements about responsible consumption
periods.activity_title: Solar and Wind — Evaluating Renewable Alternatives
periods.activity_description: Students evaluate solar and wind energy as alternatives to fossil fuels by applying the same two-criteria framework used in the previous units: which resource they replace, and whether they address the cause of fossil fuel depletion or only its consequences. They also trace the indirect solar energy pathway described in Section 11.3 — from sun to plant to animal to human.

roles.role_description: Applies the two-criteria evaluation to solar panels, solar cookers, solar water heaters, and windmills, and traces the direct and indirect solar energy pathways in a diagram.
Introduces the direct versus indirect solar energy distinction from Section 11.3, then guides groups to connect it to the evaluation criteria before releasing them to work.

time_bands.activity: The teacher introduces the direct versus indirect solar energy distinction from Section 11.3 using the cow-grazing example, and connects it to the question: 'If we switch to solar, are we fixing the cause of fossil fuel depletion or its consequence?'
Groups evaluate solar panels, solar cookers, solar water heaters, and windmills using the two-criteria grid, and sketch a direct and indirect solar energy pathway diagram.

Groups share their evaluation verdicts; the class discusses whether any solar or wind technology has limitations the chapter hints at (e.g., wind energy only where wind is available — windmill farms named in specific regions).
Students add solar and wind evaluations to the class evaluation grid started in the previous units, completing the grid across all chapter resources.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit applies the evaluation framework to energy resources, connecting the renewable alternatives back to the fossil fuel depletion causes examined in Stage 3. Students often treat solar energy as a complete solution and do not probe its limitations; use the chapter's own regional windmill farm examples — Muppandal, Jaisalmer, Brahmanvel — to surface the point that availability varies by location. The completed class evaluation grid across all resources is a strong visual summary the class will use in the synthesis unit.
materials: Class evaluation grid (from previous units)
Notebooks for solar energy pathway diagram

periods.stage_label: Evaluate conservation choices and develop informed judgements about responsible consumption
periods.activity_title: Rocks, Minerals, and Responsible Use — Irreplaceable Resources
periods.activity_description: Students evaluate the responsible use argument for rocks and minerals by examining two dimensions from the chapter: the extremely long formation time (thousands to millions of years) and the wide range of societal uses (construction, tools, mobile phones, aircraft). They write a structured judgement: is the urgency to conserve rocks and minerals equal to, greater than, or less than that for freshwater or forests?

roles.role_description: Reviews the chapter's content on rocks and minerals and writes a structured three-paragraph judgement comparing conservation urgency, using specific chapter details as evidence.
Poses the comparative judgement question, reminds students to draw only on chapter content as evidence, and circulates to challenge unsupported claims.

time_bands.activity: The teacher frames the comparative question and reminds students of the evidence available: formation time, uses, and whether the resource can be replenished — asking them to recall these from the reference table and class evaluation grid.

Students write their three-paragraph judgement: paragraph 1 — evidence for urgency from formation time; paragraph 2 — evidence from range of uses; paragraph 3 — comparative verdict with freshwater or forests, supported by chapter details.
Students exchange notebooks with a partner, who underlines one strong evidence sentence and circles one claim that needs more chapter support.
Two or three students share their comparative verdict; the class offers brief agreement or disagreement with verbal reasoning, closing Stage 4 before the synthesis unit.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit asks for the most sustained individual evaluative writing of the chapter, so it is deliberately placed as the last Stage 4 unit before the synthesis. Students frequently write that freshwater is obviously more urgent because 'we need water to survive'; push them to also engage with the mobile phone minerals argument from Section 11.5 and the millions-of-years formation time, which the chapter uses explicitly to argue for conservation. The peer-underlining and circling exchange builds accountability for evidence-based reasoning without requiring the teacher to read every notebook in real time.
materials: Reference table and class evaluation grid from previous units
Notebooks for written judgement

roles.role_description: Presents the scenario on the board and clarifies that students must draw on the full chapter's classification and conservation framework — not just one resource — in their recommendation.

Classifies each resource in the scenario as renewable or non-renewable, evaluates available conservation options for each need, and produces a group written recommendation with a minimum of three chapter-grounded justifications.
After group discussion, each student writes a personal one-paragraph reflection on which single conservation choice in the recommendation is most justified and why.

periods.activity_description: Students receive a one-page profile of a fictional inland village called Ramnagar and a set of twelve resource-decision cards. The village profile describes Ramnagar's geography, daily activities, and a list of six problems it currently faces — a drying well, heavy smoke from coal-fired brick kilns, a deforested hillside, eroding farm soil, frequent power cuts, and unequal water access between wealthier and poorer households. Each resource-decision card proposes one action the village council could take, drawn from resources the chapter covers but set entirely in this new fictional context. Working in groups, students build a written Resource Plan for Ramnagar: they select the actions they recommend, sequence them by urgency, classify every resource each action draws on as renewable or non-renewable, and write a brief justification explaining what harm each chosen action prevents or reverses. The plan is then presented to the class as a 'council report', and the class cross-examines each group's reasoning. The task is the synthesis — to build a coherent, justified plan the group must simultaneously apply the renewable/non-renewable classification, trace cause-and-effect chains between resource misuse and the village's problems, and weigh responsible use against present need, drawing every strand of the chapter into one working document.
periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis unit asks groups to build a justified Resource Plan for a fictional village, Ramnagar, drawing simultaneously on the renewable/non-renewable classification, cause-and-effect chains of resource misuse, and the principle of responsible use — forcing integration rather than topic-by-topic recall. The most important facilitation move is coaching the cross-examination audience to ask 'which of Ramnagar's six problems does this card solve, and through what resource mechanism?' rather than 'is this good or bad?'; watch also for two predictable gaps — natural gas classified as a solution to depletion rather than only pollution, and granite quarrying rejected outright rather than justified with restraint (see material). The Ramnagar village profile and twelve decision cards are prepared before class (see visual aids).
materials: One printed or hand-written Ramnagar village profile per group (see visual aid: 'Ramnagar Village Profile')
Twelve resource-decision cards per group, one sentence each on slips of paper or card (see visual aid: 'Ramnagar Decision Cards')
Student notebooks or loose sheets for writing the Resource Plan
Blackboard and chalk for tracking which of Ramnagar's six problems each group has addressed during cross-examination
Pencils or pens

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces Ramnagar by reading the village profile aloud while distributing one copy per group. Profile text (teacher writes this on slips or the board before class): 'Ramnagar is a village of about 400 families situated near a river, a granite ridge, and a hillside that was forested until ten years ago. Most families farm the land around the village. The village has: a well that is running low because the underground water is not being replenished fast enough; a row of coal-fired brick kilns whose smoke hangs over the village every morning; a hillside with almost no trees left; farm soil that washes away into the river after heavy rain; electricity that cuts out for several hours each day; and a water pipe that reaches the wealthier part of the village but not the poorer lanes.' Teacher reads the six problems aloud and writes them as a numbered list on the board. Teacher then distributes the twelve decision cards face-up and says: 'Your group is the Ramnagar village council. You have these twelve possible actions. Build a Resource Plan: choose at least seven actions, put them in order of urgency, and for each one write — which of Ramnagar's six problems it addresses, what resource it uses, whether that resource is renewable or non-renewable, and why you are recommending it.' Groups read all twelve cards silently before beginning.

Groups build their Resource Plans in notebooks. Teacher circulates, listening for reasoning quality rather than correct answers, and poses targeted prompts: to a group that has accepted natural gas (card 4) without comment — 'You've noted it is less polluting than coal; what about its replenishment time compared to solar?' To a group that has skipped the stepwell (card 3) — 'Ramnagar's well is running low; which of your chosen cards addresses that problem directly?' To a group that has left out granite quarrying (card 8) — 'The chapter describes rocks being used for construction; does responsible use mean never quarrying, or something else?' Teacher does not correct groups but keeps their reasoning moving toward precision. Groups must write at least one sentence of justification per chosen card before the presentation phase begins.

Each group nominates one spokesperson. Groups present their Resource Plans in rapid succession — approximately ninety seconds per group — stating only their top three urgency choices and their reasoning. After each presentation, the class cross-examines for ninety seconds: the teacher directs the audience to ask only questions of the form 'which of the six problems does this card solve, and through what resource mechanism?' Teacher marks on the board which of Ramnagar's six problems have been addressed across all groups, and which — if any — remain unaddressed. If a problem is still unaddressed after all presentations, teacher asks the whole class: 'Which card or cards would handle this, and why did groups leave it out?'

Teacher draws the unit closed by naming what the task itself demonstrated: to build even one workable plan for Ramnagar required using the renewable/non-renewable classification to choose between options, tracing how each resource problem arose from a specific kind of misuse or overuse, recognising that non-renewable resources can be used responsibly rather than not at all, and seeing that the village's problems — smoke, soil erosion, water shortage, power cuts, unequal access — are not separate; they are linked because all of them trace back to how natural resources are managed. Teacher points to the board's list of Ramnagar's six problems and says: 'Every concept in this chapter was working inside your plan. That is what the chapter is for.' No further summary is given.

visual_aids.title: Ramnagar Village Profile
visual_aids.text: Ramnagar is a village of about 400 families situated near a river, a granite ridge, and a hillside that was forested until ten years ago. Most families farm the land around the village. The village has: a well that is running low because the underground water is not being replenished fast enough; a row of coal-fired brick kilns whose smoke hangs over the village every morning; a hillside with almost no trees left; farm soil that washes away into the river after heavy rain; electricity that cuts out for several hours each day; and a water pipe that reaches the wealthier part of the village but not the poorer lanes.

visual_aids.title: Ramnagar Decision Cards
visual_aids.table:
Card | Proposal
1 | Install rooftop solar panels on the school
2 | Plant a community forest on the deforested hillside
3 | Build a small stepwell to harvest monsoon rain
4 | Switch the brick kilns from coal to natural gas
5 | Introduce CNG three-wheelers for transport
6 | Create a village compost pit using fallen leaves
7 | Use wind energy to pump water from the existing well
8 | Quarry the local granite ridge for new construction material
9 | Ask residents to fix all household tap leaks
10 | Organise a Van Mahotsav tree-planting drive
11 | Install a solar water heater at the community centre
12 | Restrict the number of trees felled each year

visual_aids.title: Decision Cards — selection rules
visual_aids.text: Groups must choose at least seven cards and may choose all twelve. Every chosen card requires a written justification. Each of Ramnagar's six problems must be matched to at least one chosen card — this prevents groups from avoiding uncomfortable options.

visual_aids.title: Ramnagar's Six Problems — Board Tracking Grid
visual_aids.table:
Problem | Problem Description | Addressed by Card(s)
1 | Well running low — groundwater not replenished fast enough | 
2 | Coal-fired brick kilns — smoke hangs over village each morning | 
3 | Hillside almost entirely deforested | 
4 | Farm soil washing into the river after heavy rain | 
5 | Electricity cuts out for several hours each day | 
6 | Water pipe reaches wealthier households but not poorer lanes |

visual_aids.title: Teacher Prompts for Two Predictable Gaps
visual_aids.text:
Gap A — Natural gas (Card 4) accepted without critique: prompt with 'You've noted it is less polluting than coal; what about its replenishment time compared to solar? Does this solve the depletion problem or only the pollution problem?'

Gap B — Granite quarrying (Card 8) rejected outright: prompt with 'The chapter describes rocks being used for construction; does responsible use mean never quarrying, or something else?' The correct move is to justify quarrying while noting the need for restraint — not to ban it.

assessment_items.question_text: A student holds their breath during the Activity 11.1 exercise and notices discomfort within a short time. What does this observation most directly show about air?

options.label: A
options.text: Air contains more nitrogen than any other gas, and nitrogen is what the body needs urgently.

options.label: B
options.text: Moving air called wind is what causes the body to feel discomfort when breathing stops.

options.label: C
options.text: The body requires a continuous supply of air because it cannot function without the oxygen air contains.

options.label: D
options.text: The discomfort shows that carbon dioxide builds up immediately and replaces all the oxygen in the lungs.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student confuses the most abundant gas in air (nitrogen, 78%) with the gas the body urgently needs (oxygen, 21%), showing a misconception about the composition of air from Section 11.1.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student conflates the chapter's second air concept — wind as moving air — with the breath-holding observation, showing confusion between two ideas introduced in the same section.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student applies a plausible but inaccurate detail — carbon dioxide does build up, but it does not immediately replace all oxygen — indicating recall of a related but overstated detail from the section.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with the text-heavy stem can be supported by the teacher re-enacting the breath-holding moment before presenting the question. Students who answer quickly can be asked to explain why each incorrect option is wrong in one sentence.

assessment_items.question_text: A student records soil observations in the table provided. Refer to the table provided. Which statement best explains why the three samples look and feel different from each other?

options.label: A
options.text: All soils start identical but change colour based on how wet they are at the time of collection.

options.label: B
options.text: The colour differences show which soils have more air trapped in them and which have less.

options.label: C
options.text: The samples come from different locations and therefore contain different materials.

options.label: D
options.text: The texture difference is caused only by how the student rubbed the soil, not by the soil itself.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student believes moisture at collection time determines colour, not composition — a misconception about what soil observation records, not grounded in the chapter's Activity 11.4 explanation.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student attributes the observation to the observer's action rather than the soil's properties, showing a confusion between the procedure of observation and the property being observed.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student imports an air-related concept from Section 11.1 into the soil context, showing a cross-section confusion between two resources studied in the same unit.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find the table difficult to process can be supported by having the teacher read each row aloud. Students who answer quickly can be asked to name one more difference they would expect if a fourth sample came from a riverbank.

assessment_items.question_text: A student classifies soil as renewable because 'it comes from nature and nature can make more.' Why is this classification incorrect according to the chapter?

options.label: A
options.text: All resources that come from nature are renewable, so the student's classification is actually correct.

options.label: B
options.text: Soil cannot be classified as renewable because it does not come from the Sun the way plants and wind do.

options.label: C
options.text: Soil forms over thousands of years through the action of the Sun, water, and living organisms, so it is not replenished within a reasonable time and is classified as non-renewable.

options.label: D
options.text: Soil is not a natural resource at all — it is made by humans through farming and composting.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student denies soil's status as a natural resource entirely — a fundamental misconception contradicting the chapter's Section 11.5 opening statement.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student applies a solar-energy criterion — 'coming from the Sun' — as the test for renewability, confusing the solar energy classification from Section 11.3 with the replenishment-time criterion from Section 11.7.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student accepts the prompt's flawed reasoning without critique, revealing that the replenishment-time criterion for renewability has not been distinguished from the 'comes from nature' criterion — the most common Stage 2 misconception.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with the negatively framed stem ('why is this incorrect') can be supported by the teacher rephrasing: 'What is missing from the student's reason?' Students who answer correctly can be asked to apply the same replenishment-time test to minerals.

Activity step | Resources used
Boiling rice on a gas stove | LPG, water, electricity

assessment_items.question_text: Refer to the table provided. A student maps their morning routine and lists the resources used in each step. Which step in the morning routine uses the highest number of non-renewable resources?

options.label: A
options.text: Boiling rice on a gas stove

options.label: B
options.text: Driving to school in a diesel car

options.label: C
options.text: Ironing clothes with an electric iron

options.label: D
options.text: Watering the garden with a hose

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student identifies LPG as non-renewable but overlooks that water is renewable and electricity here is from a coal (non-renewable) source — and misses that diesel driving uses both diesel and rock-derived road, giving it more non-renewable resources overall.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student stops at electricity without tracing it to its coal source, and does not count a second non-renewable resource in the step — showing partial application of the classification framework.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may classify water as non-renewable (a Stage 2 misconception) or may count hose material without recognising that water is renewable, arriving at a miscount.

assessment_items.question_text: A student says: 'Forests are non-renewable because once you cut the trees, they are gone.' Using the chapter's definition of renewable and non-renewable resources, explain why this statement is incorrect and classify forests correctly with a reason.
expected_elements: States that a renewable resource is one that is renewed, replenished, or restored by natural processes within a reasonable period of time.
Applies this definition to forests: new forests can grow, so forests are renewable.
Identifies what the student's reasoning got wrong: confusing the fact that cut trees are gone with the fact that the resource as a whole can be replenished.
Acknowledges, based on the chapter, that forest cover is declining due to large-scale cutting but this does not change the classification — it makes conservation more urgent.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who struggle to organise their response can be prompted with two sentence starters: 'The chapter defines a renewable resource as...' and 'The student's error is...' Students who respond quickly can be asked to identify one non-renewable resource that students most commonly misclassify as renewable and explain why.

assessment_items.question_text: The chapter states that burning fossil fuels releases smoke and carbon dioxide. Which of the following best describes the consequence of this release on the environment, as described in the chapter?

options.label: A
options.text: Carbon dioxide dissolves in rivers, making freshwater saline and unfit for drinking.

options.label: B
options.text: The carbon dioxide released directly decomposes minerals in rocks, causing them to crumble faster.

options.label: C
options.text: The release contributes to large-scale air pollution.

options.label: D
options.text: The smoke causes the Sun's energy to be blocked, which stops plants from photosynthesising entirely.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student links smoke to photosynthesis — connecting two chapter concepts (fossil fuels and solar energy/photosynthesis) but overstating the consequence in a way the chapter does not support, showing cross-section confusion.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student conflates air pollution and water pollution, incorrectly routing a consequence from Section 11.6 into Section 11.2, indicating a failure to distinguish the chapter's resource-specific cause-effect chains.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student connects carbon dioxide to rock decomposition — an invented causal link not present in the chapter — indicating construction of a plausible-sounding but unsupported consequence.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find the multi-option analysis difficult can be supported by being asked to locate the relevant sentence in Section 11.6 before choosing. Students who answer quickly can be asked to extend the chain: what happens to people when large-scale air pollution occurs?

assessment_items.question_text: The chapter says that forest cover has been declining due to large-scale cutting of trees. Which of the following correctly identifies a consequence of this decline for animals, as described in the chapter?

options.label: A
options.text: Animals begin to depend on fossil fuels as an alternative energy source when forests disappear.

options.label: B
options.text: Animals migrate to coastal areas where saline water is available, since freshwater dries up with forests.

options.label: C
options.text: Fallen leaves can no longer decompose on the forest floor, so soil nutrients increase sharply.

options.label: D
options.text: Wild animals, birds, and insects lose the food and shelter that forests provide, threatening their survival.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student invents a cross-resource dependency — animals using fossil fuels — that the chapter does not state, indicating a failure to stay within chapter content when constructing causal chains.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student reverses the decomposition consequence described in Section 11.4: the chapter says fallen leaves enrich soil; this option incorrectly claims their absence increases nutrients, showing a detail-recall error within the forest section.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student links forest loss to saline coastal water — combining details from Sections 11.4 and 11.2 in an unsupported causal link, indicating cross-section confusion under causal reasoning.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle to hold both 'forest loss' and 'animal consequence' simultaneously can be prompted to re-read the one sentence in Section 11.4 that names forests as natural habitats. Students who answer quickly can be asked to name the specific living beings the chapter lists as depending on forests.

assessment_items.question_text: Construct a cause-and-effect chain for freshwater using the chapter's content. Start from 'freshwater is wasted or polluted' and end at a named social consequence. Your chain must have at least three linked steps.
expected_elements: Identifies that freshwater available for use is a very small fraction of Earth's total water, as the chapter states.
Links wastage or pollution of this small fraction to reduced availability of clean freshwater.
Names a social consequence: unequal access across India, inability to use water for drinking, agriculture, or industrial use.
Chain is presented in a logical sequence with each step following from the previous (not just a list of disconnected facts).

SCR.inclusivity: Students who struggle to construct the chain can be given the first step written out and asked to complete the remaining steps. Students who respond quickly can be asked to add a fourth step that names a conservation action that could interrupt the chain.

assessment_items.question_text: The chapter describes the Chipko movement, in which local women hugged trees to prevent them from being felled. Evaluating this conservation practice using the chapter's framework, which statement best describes what the Chipko movement addresses?

options.label: A
options.text: It addresses fossil fuel depletion by reducing the need for wood as a fuel source.

options.label: B
options.text: It addresses soil erosion, which is the main consequence of removing trees from a forest.

options.label: C
options.text: It addresses the cause of forest loss by preventing trees from being cut in the first place.

options.label: D
options.text: It addresses the consequence of forest loss by planting new trees to replace those already cut.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student confuses the Chipko movement with Van Mahotsav — both are forest conservation efforts in the chapter but with different mechanisms; this shows confusion between two chapter conservation practices.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student connects forest protection to fossil fuel conservation — an unsupported cross-resource link not made in the chapter — showing a failure to evaluate the practice within its specific resource context.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student identifies soil erosion as the primary consequence the Chipko movement addresses — a plausible environmental link but not what the chapter states; this shows recall of a related but incorrect detail about the consequence of tree removal.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with the cause-versus-consequence distinction can be prompted to ask: 'Does this action stop the problem before it happens, or clean up after?' Students who answer quickly can be asked to apply the same evaluation to Van Mahotsav and compare the two.

assessment_items.question_text: A student argues that walking or cycling instead of driving is more effective than using a solar cooker for reducing fossil fuel depletion. Which evaluation best assesses this argument using the chapter's evidence?

options.label: A
options.text: The argument is correct because vehicles are the only major user of fossil fuels mentioned in the chapter, making transport reduction the only relevant action.

options.label: B
options.text: The argument is irrelevant because fossil fuels are renewable and will be replenished before current supplies run out.

options.label: C
options.text: The argument is reasonable because both practices reduce fossil fuel use, but walking or cycling reduces petrol or diesel consumption directly while solar cookers reduce LPG or coal use for cooking — the chapter presents both as valid actions to reduce dependence.

options.label: D
options.text: The argument is wrong because solar cookers directly replace cooking fuel, which is a larger share of fossil fuel use than vehicle fuel.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student invents a quantitative comparison — 'larger share of fossil fuel use' — that the chapter does not provide, showing a tendency to fabricate evidence rather than evaluate within the chapter's scope.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student misreads the chapter by claiming vehicles are the only fossil fuel users, overlooking the chapter's explicit mention of coal for electricity and natural gas for cooking — a recall error within Stage 3's content.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student misclassifies fossil fuels as renewable — the most fundamental Stage 2 error carried forward into Stage 4, indicating the renewable or non-renewable classification has not been secured.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find the multi-step evaluation complex can be supported by the teacher isolating the question: 'What fuels does walking reduce? What fuels does a solar cooker reduce?' before asking them to compare. Students who answer quickly can be asked to identify which chapter location names specific actions to reduce fossil fuel dependence.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can evaluate at least two conservation practices from the chapter by stating which resource each conserves and whether it addresses the cause or consequence of depletion, and can produce a written judgement comparing the conservation urgency of different resource types with chapter-grounded evidence.

assessment_items.question_text: The chapter describes rainwater harvesting as an age-old conservation practice in India and gives the example of traditional stepwells — Bawadi in Rajasthan and Vav in Gujarat. It also describes Van Mahotsav as a week-long national festival in July during which new trees are planted. Evaluate these two conservation practices: for each, state which resource it conserves, whether it addresses the cause or consequence of the resource problem, and which practice you judge to be more effective and why. Your response must use specific evidence from the chapter.
look_for: Correctly identifies rainwater harvesting as conserving freshwater and explains it as addressing the cause — capturing rainwater before it is lost rather than reacting after shortage occurs.
Correctly identifies Van Mahotsav as addressing a consequence — replanting after forest cover has been lost — rather than preventing the original cutting.
States a clear verdict on relative effectiveness and justifies it with reference to the cause-versus-consequence distinction.
Uses at least one specific chapter detail (stepwells, Bawadi or Vav, Rajasthan or Gujarat, July planting, Chipko movement as contrast) as evidence for the judgement.
Avoids fabricating details not in the chapter — evaluation stays within the chapter's evidence base.

ECR.inclusivity: Students who find the dual-practice comparison demanding can be supported by answering the three questions for one practice at a time before comparing. Students with strong responses can be challenged to name a third chapter conservation practice and place it on the cause-to-consequence spectrum.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify and evaluate a set of natural resources in an unfamiliar scenario, and produce a justified recommendation about responsible consumption that weighs immediate community needs against long-term sustainability, drawing on the chapter's content as evidence.

competency.competency_text: Judicious consumption of resources and mitigation of climate change

assessment_items.question_text: A community generates all its cooking energy from coal and all its drinking water from a river. Which of the following correctly classifies these two resources and identifies the more urgent conservation concern?

options.label: A
options.text: Both coal and river water are non-renewable; coal is more urgent because water can be recycled.

options.label: B
options.text: Both resources are renewable because nature provides both of them; the community can continue using both without restriction.

options.label: C
options.text: Coal is non-renewable and river water is renewable; coal conservation is more urgent because coal takes millions of years to form and cannot be replenished within a reasonable time.

options.label: D
options.text: Coal is renewable because it comes from ancient plants, which are a natural source; river water is non-renewable because rivers can dry up.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student misclassifies river water as non-renewable — a persistent Stage 2 error carried into the synthesis, indicating the replenishment-time criterion for freshwater has not been secured.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student applies origin logic (coal from ancient plants = natural = renewable) rather than replenishment-time logic, showing that the cause-of-classification reasoning has not displaced the 'comes from nature' misconception addressed in Stage 2.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student reverts to the most fundamental Stage 2 misconception — 'provided by nature = renewable' — applying it to both resources simultaneously, indicating the classification framework has not been internalised.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who hesitate can be prompted to recall the formation-time difference between river water and coal from their reference table. Students who answer quickly can be asked to identify a third resource from the scenario and classify it with a reason.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify and evaluate a set of natural resources in an unfamiliar scenario, and produce a justified recommendation about responsible consumption that weighs immediate community needs against long-term sustainability, drawing on the chapter's content as evidence.

competency.competency_text: Judicious consumption of resources and mitigation of climate change

assessment_items.question_text: A community plans to replace its diesel vehicles with vehicles powered by solar energy. Using the chapter's framework, which evaluation of this plan is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: The plan is ineffective because solar energy is a renewable resource and renewable resources cannot power vehicles.

options.label: B
options.text: The plan is unnecessary because diesel is also produced from natural sources underground and will be replenished over time.

options.label: C
options.text: The plan only addresses air pollution as a consequence and does not reduce fossil fuel use because vehicles still need roads made from rock.

options.label: D
options.text: The plan reduces dependence on a non-renewable resource (diesel from petroleum) and replaces it with a renewable resource (solar energy), addressing the cause of fossil fuel depletion.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student correctly identifies solar as renewable but incorrectly infers it cannot power vehicles — an unsupported conclusion that contradicts the chapter's description of solar panels generating electricity, including for transport.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student applies a formation-source argument ('produced from natural sources') to classify diesel as renewable — a version of the 'comes from nature = renewable' misconception the chapter explicitly rejects in its treatment of fossil fuels.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student correctly identifies air pollution as a consequence but then incorrectly argues that roads negate the fossil fuel saving — combining a valid causal link (road use) with an unjustified conclusion, showing partial causal reasoning.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find the multi-dimension evaluation complex can be supported by being asked to first classify diesel and solar separately before evaluating the switch. Students who answer quickly can be asked to identify one limitation the chapter hints at for solar-powered vehicles.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify and evaluate a set of natural resources in an unfamiliar scenario, and produce a justified recommendation about responsible consumption that weighs immediate community needs against long-term sustainability, drawing on the chapter's content as evidence.

competency.competency_text: Judicious consumption of resources and mitigation of climate change

assessment_items.question_text: A small town currently relies on coal for electricity, draws drinking water from a nearby lake, cuts trees from the adjacent forest for construction timber, and quarries granite from a local hill for building. The town council wants to continue meeting all four needs for the next fifty years. Using the chapter's classification and evaluation framework, identify which of these resource uses is most likely to become unsustainable first, and recommend one specific change the town should make. Justify your recommendation with evidence from the chapter.
look_for: Correctly classifies all four resources — coal (non-renewable, millions of years to form), lake water (renewable), forest timber (renewable but slow to regrow), granite (non-renewable, thousands to millions of years to form) — with the classification criterion stated.
Identifies coal or granite as most likely to become unsustainable first and provides a formation-time reason drawn from the chapter.

Makes a specific, named recommendation (e.g., replace coal with solar energy, replace granite quarrying with an alternative building material mentioned in the chapter such as laterite or slate) grounded in chapter content.
Justifies the recommendation by linking it to the cause of the sustainability problem, not merely its consequence.
Avoids fabricating details — all evidence is traceable to chapter sections.

ECR.inclusivity: Students who find the four-resource comparison overwhelming can be supported by being asked to classify each resource one at a time before comparing formation times. Students who respond strongly can be asked to evaluate whether their recommended change addresses the cause or the consequence of the sustainability problem.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify and evaluate a set of natural resources in an unfamiliar scenario, and produce a justified recommendation about responsible consumption that weighs immediate community needs against long-term sustainability, drawing on the chapter's content as evidence.

competency.competency_text: Judicious consumption of resources and mitigation of climate change

assessment_items.task: A hill community has access to five resources listed in the table provided. The community must meet its needs for the next thirty years without destroying any resource permanently. Use the table to classify each resource, identify a conservation option from the chapter for each, evaluate whether that option addresses the cause or consequence of depletion, and record your verdict. Then, in the space below the table, write two to three sentences recommending which single change would most improve the community's long-term resource security, and explain why using evidence from the chapter.
assessment_items.scaffold: Complete the table row by row: first write renewable or non-renewable, then name the conservation option from the chapter, then write cause or consequence, then your verdict. When you reach the written recommendation, begin with: 'The single most important change is...' and support your choice with one specific detail from the chapter.
format_of_output: Completed table with all five rows filled
Two to three sentence written recommendation with at least one chapter-specific detail as evidence

OPEN_TASK.format_type: Classification or sorting task with justification
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The Final Stage implied LO requires students to classify resources and evaluate conservation choices simultaneously in an unfamiliar scenario — the classification-with-justification format is the most direct demonstration vehicle for this integrated cognitive operation.
OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: A complete response demonstrates the student's ability to apply the renewable or non-renewable classification criterion to novel resource instances, select and evaluate conservation options from the chapter's evidence base, and produce a reasoned judgement that weighs immediate need against long-term sustainability across multiple resource types simultaneously.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The table forces a structured four-step evaluation for each resource before the written recommendation, preventing students from jumping to a conclusion without classification and conservation evidence. The 'cause or consequence' column is the highest-order cell — a student who fills it correctly has demonstrated Stage 4 evaluation carried into Stage 5. The written recommendation is where individual reasoning becomes visible; look for whether the student's chosen change is connected to a cause (preventing depletion) rather than only a consequence (repairing damage).
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong responses: correctly classify all five resources with the replenishment-time criterion; name a specific chapter conservation option (not a generic suggestion); correctly label cause or consequence; write a recommendation that cites a named chapter detail (e.g., solar panels, stepwells, Van Mahotsav) and links it to the cause of the resource problem. Weak responses: classify resources by 'found in nature' rather than replenishment time; invent conservation options not in the chapter; label all options as addressing 'cause' without distinguishing; write a recommendation without any chapter-specific evidence.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find the five-row table too large can complete any three rows of their choosing and still write the recommendation — the cognitive operation is demonstrated even over three resources. Students who complete the table quickly can be asked to add a sixth row for a resource of their own choosing from the chapter and evaluate it by the same criteria. Students who struggle with the written recommendation can be supported by the sentence starter in the scaffold.
